hints: Look closely at the structure and count the different types of $\text{-OH}$ groups present in tartaric acid.
Tartaric acid has two carboxylic acid $\text{-COOH}$ groups and two alcohol $\text{-OH}$ groups, so think about which reagent reacts with both types.
Remember sodium metal reacts with both acids and alcohols to release hydrogen, while bases and carbonates only neutralise the acidic carboxyl groups, so work out which gives a 4 to 1 ratio.
walkthrough:
**Identify the functional groups**

Look at the structure with care. Tartaric acid is $\text{HOOC-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-COOH}$.

That means per molecule: $$2 \times \text{carboxylic acid (-COOH) + 2 } \times \text{ alcohol (-OH)}$$

**Recall reactivity toward sodium**

Sodium is a very reactive metal. It reacts with any $\text{O-H}$ bond that has even slightly acidic hydrogen.

$$2\text{R-COOH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{R-COONa} + \text{H}_2$$
$$2\text{R-OH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{R-ONa} + \text{H}_2$$

**Recall reactivity toward bases and carbonates**

Sodium hydroxide, sodium carbonate and sodium hydrogencarbonate are bases. They only neutralise the strongly acidic carboxylic acid groups, not the weakly acidic alcohol groups.

So 1 mole of tartaric acid with 2 $\text{-COOH}$ groups needs only 2 moles $\text{NaOH}$, 2 moles $\text{NaHCO}_3$, or 1 mole $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$.

**Match the 4 to 1 ratio**

Only sodium reacts with all four $\text{O-H}$ groups.

$$1 \text{ mole acid } \times (2 + 2) = 4 \text{ moles Na needed}$$

options.A: Correct. Sodium reacts with both carboxylic acids and alcohols. With 2 $\text{-COOH}$ plus 2 alcoholic $\text{-OH}$ groups, one mole of tartaric acid consumes four moles of Na, giving hydrogen gas in each case.
options.B: Incorrect. Sodium carbonate only reacts with carboxylic acids, not alcohols. The equation is $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + 2\text{R-COOH} \rightarrow 2\text{R-COONa} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, so 1 mole of tartaric acid needs only 1 mole of carbonate, not 4.
options.C: Incorrect. Sodium hydrogencarbonate only neutralises carboxylic acids: $\text{NaHCO}_3 + \text{R-COOH} \rightarrow \text{R-COONa} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Two $\text{-COOH}$ groups need only 2 moles, and the alcohol groups do not react.
options.D: Incorrect. Sodium hydroxide neutralises only the carboxylic acid groups: $\text{NaOH} + \text{R-COOH} \rightarrow \text{R-COONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Two $\text{-COOH}$ groups need only 2 moles of NaOH, as alcohols are too weakly acidic to react.
